##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of mind/consciousness/Dementia.md
```markdown
# Dementia
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bf/A_man_diagnosed_as_suffering_from_acute_dementia._Lithograph_Wellcome_L0026694.jpg)
- [[Dementia]] is the general name for a decline in [[Cognition | cognitive]] abilities that impacts a person's ability to perform  [[Activities of daily living | everyday activities]]. This typically involves problems with [[Memory | memory]], [[Thought | thinking]], and [[Behavior | behavior]]. Aside from [[Amnesia | memory impairment]] and a **disruption in** **thought** **patterns**, the most common symptoms include emotional problems, difficulties with language, and decreased [[Motivation | motivation]].  The symptoms may be described as occurring in a [[Continuum (measurement) | continuum]] over several stages. Dementia ultimately has a significant effect on the individual, [[Caregiver | caregivers]], and on social relationships in general. A diagnosis of dementia requires the observation of a change from a person's usual mental functioning and a greater [[Cognition | cognitive]] decline than what is caused by normal [[Ageing | aging]].
- Several diseases and injuries to the brain such as a stroke can give rise to [[Dementia | dementia]]. However, the most common cause is [[Alzheimer's disease]], a [[Neurodegenerative disease | neurodegenerative disorder]]. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition ([[DSM-5]]), has re-described dementia as either a mild or major neurocognitive disorder with varying degrees of severity and many [[Etiology | causative]] subtypes. The [[International Classification of Diseases]] ([[ICD-11]]) also classes dementia as a neurocognitive disorder (NCD) with many forms or subclasses. [[Dementia]] is listed as an acquired brain syndrome, marked by a decline in cognitive function, and is contrasted with [[Neurodevelopmental disorder | neurodevelopmental disorders]]. Dementia is also described as a spectrum of disorders with causative subtypes of dementia based on a known disorder, such as [[Parkinson's disease]], for [[Parkinson's disease dementia]]; [[Huntington's disease]], for Huntington's disease [[Dementia | dementia]]; [[Vascular disease | vascular disease]], for [[Vascular dementia | vascular dementia]]; [[HIV/AIDS | HIV infection]], causing [[HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder | HIV dementia]]; [[Frontotemporal lobar degeneration | frontotemporal lobar degeneration]] for [[Frontotemporal dementia | frontotemporal dementia]]; or [[Lewy body dementias | Lewy body disease]] for [[Dementia with Lewy bodies | dementia with Lewy bodies]], and [[Prion | prion diseases]]. Subtypes of neurodegenerative dementias may also be based on the underlying pathology of misfolded proteins such as [[Synucleinopathy | synucleinopathies]], and [[Tauopathy | tauopathies]]. More than one type of dementia existing together is known as [[Dementia | mixed dementia]].
- Many neurocognitive disorders may be caused by another medical condition or disorder that includes brain tumours, and [[Subdural hematoma | subdural hematoma]]; [[Endocrine disease | endocrine disorders]] such as [[Hypothyroidism | hypothyroidism]], and [[Hypoglycemia | hypoglycemia]]; [[Malnutrition | nutritional deficiencies]] including [[Thiamine | thiamine]], and [[Niacin | niacin]]; infections, immune disorders, liver or kidney failure, [[Metabolic disorder | metabolic disorders]] such as [[Kufs disease]], and some [[Leukodystrophy | leukodystrophies]], and [[Neurological disorder | neurological disorders]] such as [[Epilepsy | epilepsy]], and [[Multiple sclerosis | multiple sclerosis]]. Some of the neurocognitive deficits may sometimes show improvement with treatment of the medical condition.
- Diagnosis is usually based on [[Medical history | history of the illness]] and [[Cognitive test | cognitive testing]] with [[Neuroimaging | imaging]]. [[Blood test | Blood tests]] may be taken to rule out other possible causes that may be reversible, such as [[Hypothyroidism | hypothyroidism]] (an underactive thyroid), and to determine the dementia subtype. One commonly used [[Cognitive test | cognitive test]] is the [[Mini–mental state examination | mini–mental state examination]]. The greatest risk factor for developing [[Dementia | dementia]] is [[Ageing | aging]], however dementia is not a normal part of aging. Many people aged 90 and above show no signs of dementia. Several risk factors for [[Dementia | dementia]], such as smoking and [[Obesity | obesity]], are preventable by lifestyle changes. [[Screening (medicine) | Screening]] the general older population for the disorder is not seen to affect the outcome.
- Dementia is currently the seventh leading cause of death worldwide and has 10 million new cases reported every year (one every ~3 seconds). There is no known [[Cure | cure]] for dementia. [[Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor | Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors]] such as [[Donepezil | donepezil]] are often used and may be beneficial in mild to moderate disorder. The overall benefit, however, may be minor. There are many measures that can improve the quality of life of people with [[Dementia | dementia]] and their caregivers. [[Cognitive behavioral therapy | Cognitive and behavioral interventions]] may be appropriate for treating associated symptoms of depression.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of mind/Philosophy of mind.md
```markdown
# Philosophy of mind
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9b/Philbar_4.png)
- [[Philosophy]] of [[Mind | mind]] is a branch of [[Philosophy | philosophy]] that studies the [[Ontology | ontology]] and nature of the [[Mind | mind]] and its relationship with the body. The [[Mind–body problem | mind–body problem]] is a paradigmatic issue in philosophy of mind, although a number of other issues are addressed, such as the [[Hard problem of consciousness | hard problem of consciousness]] and the nature of particular mental states. Aspects of the [[Mind | mind]] that are studied include [[Mental event | mental events]], mental functions, [[Mental state | mental properties]], [[Consciousness | consciousness]] and [[Neural correlates of consciousness | its neural correlates]], the [[Ontology | ontology]] of the mind, the nature of [[Cognition | cognition]] and of [[Thought | thought]], and the relationship of the [[Mind | mind]] to the body.
- [[Mind–body dualism | Dualism]] and [[Monism | monism]] are the two central [[School of thought | schools of thought]] on the [[Mind–body problem | mind–body problem]], although nuanced views have arisen that do not fit one or the other category neatly.
- Most modern philosophers of [[Mind | mind]] adopt either a [[Physicalism | reductive physicalist]] or non-reductive physicalist position, maintaining in their different ways that the mind is not something separate from the body. These approaches have been particularly influential in the sciences, especially in the fields of [[Sociobiology | sociobiology]], [[Computer science | computer science]] (specifically, [[Artificial intelligence | artificial intelligence]]), [[Evolutionary psychology | evolutionary psychology]] and the various [[Neuroscience | neurosciences]]. Reductive physicalists assert that all mental states and properties will eventually be explained by scientific accounts of physiological processes and states. Non-reductive physicalists argue that although the mind is not a separate substance, mental properties [[Supervenience | supervene]] on physical properties, or that the predicates and vocabulary used in mental descriptions and explanations are indispensable, and cannot be reduced to the language and lower-level explanations of physical science. Continued neuroscientific progress has helped to clarify some of these issues; however, they are far from being resolved.  Modern philosophers of [[Mind | mind]] continue to ask how the subjective qualities and the [[Intentionality | intentionality]] of mental states and properties can be explained in naturalistic terms.
- However, a number of issues have  been recognized with non-reductive [[Physicalism | physicalism]]. First, it is irreconcilable with self-identity over time. Secondly, intentional states of [[Consciousness | consciousness]] do not make sense on non-reductive physicalism. Thirdly, free will is impossible to reconcile with either reductive or non-reductive physicalism. Fourthly, it fails to properly explain the [[Problem of mental causation | phenomenon of mental causation]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/Philosophy of physics/Big Bang.md
```markdown
# Big Bang
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6f/CMB_Timeline300_no_WMAP.jpg)
- The Big Bang event is a [[Theoretical physics | physical theory]] that describes how the [[Expansion of the universe | universe expanded]] from an initial state of high [[Energy density | density]] and [[Temperature | temperature]]. It was first proposed in 1927 by [[Priesthood in the Catholic Church | Roman Catholic priest]] and [[Physicist | physicist]] [[Georges Lemaître]]. Various [[Physical cosmology | cosmological models]] of the Big Bang explain the evolution of the [[Observable universe | observable universe]] from the [[Planck units | earliest known periods]] through its subsequent large-scale form. These models offer a comprehensive explanation for a broad range of observed phenomena, including the abundance of [[Chemical element | light elements]], the [[Cosmic microwave background | cosmic microwave background]] (CMB) [[Electromagnetic radiation | radiation]], and large-scale structure. The overall uniformity of the [[Universe]], known as the [[Flatness problem | flatness problem]], is explained through [[Inflation (cosmology) | cosmic inflation]]: a sudden and very rapid expansion of space during the earliest moments. However, physics currently lacks a widely accepted theory of [[Quantum gravity | quantum gravity]] that can successfully model the earliest conditions of the Big Bang.
- Crucially, these models are compatible with the [[Hubble's law | Hubble–Lemaître law]]—the observation that the farther away a [[Galaxy | galaxy]] is, the faster it is moving away from Earth. Extrapolating this cosmic expansion backwards in time using the known [[Scientific law | laws of physics]], the models describe an increasingly concentrated cosmos preceded by a singularity in which [[Spacetime | space and time]] lose meaning (typically named "the Big Bang singularity"). In 1964 the CMB was discovered, which convinced many cosmologists that the competing [[Steady-state model | steady-state model]] of cosmic evolution was [[Falsifiability | falsified]], since the Big Bang models predict a uniform background radiation caused by high temperatures and densities in the distant past. A wide range of empirical evidence strongly favors the Big Bang event, which is now essentially universally accepted. Detailed measurements of the expansion rate of the [[Universe | universe]] place the Big Bang singularity at an estimated  [[1,000,000,000 | billion]] years ago, which is considered the [[Age of the universe | age of the universe]].
- There remain aspects of the observed universe that are not yet adequately explained by the Big Bang models. After its initial expansion, the [[Universe | universe]] cooled sufficiently to allow the formation of [[Subatomic particle | subatomic particles]], and later [[Atom | atoms]]. The unequal abundances of matter and [[Antimatter | antimatter]] that allowed this to occur is an unexplained effect known as [[Baryon asymmetry | baryon asymmetry]]. These primordial elements—mostly [[Hydrogen | hydrogen]], with some [[Helium | helium]] and [[Lithium | lithium]]—later coalesced through [[Gravity | gravity]], forming early [[Star | stars]] and galaxies. Astronomers observe the gravitational effects of an unknown [[Dark matter | dark matter]] surrounding galaxies. Most of the [[Gravitational potential | gravitational potential]] in the universe seems to be in this form, and the Big Bang models and various observations indicate that this excess [[Gravitational potential | gravitational potential]] is not created by [[Baryon | baryonic matter]], such as normal atoms. Measurements of the redshifts of [[Type Ia supernova | supernovae]] indicate that the **expansion of the universe is accelerating**, an observation attributed to an unexplained phenomenon known as [[Dark energy | dark energy]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/Philosophy of physics/Inflation (cosmology).md
```markdown
# Inflation (cosmology)
- In [[Physical cosmology | physical cosmology]], cosmic inflation, cosmological inflation, or just inflation, is a theory of exponential [[Expansion of the universe | expansion of space]] in the early [[Universe | universe]]. The [[Inflationary epoch | inflationary epoch]] is believed to have lasted from 10 seconds to between 10 and 10 seconds  after the [[Big Bang]]. Following the inflationary period, the [[Universe | universe]] continued to expand, but at a slower rate. The acceleration of this expansion due to [[Dark energy | dark energy]] began after the universe was already over 7.7 billion years old (5.4 billion years ago).
- Inflation theory was developed in the late 1970s and early 80s, with notable contributions by several [[Theoretical physics | theoretical physicists]], including [[Alexei Starobinsky]]  at [[Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics]], [[Alan Guth]] at [[Cornell University]], and [[Andrei Linde]] at [[Lebedev Physical Institute]]. Alexei Starobinsky, Alan Guth, and Andrei Linde won the 2014 [[Kavli Prize]] "for pioneering the theory of cosmic inflation". It was developed further in the early 1980s. It explains the origin of the [[Observable universe | large-scale structure of the cosmos]]. [[Quantum fluctuation | Quantum fluctuations]] in the microscopic inflationary region, magnified to cosmic size, become the seeds for the growth of structure in the [[Universe]] (see [[Galaxy formation and evolution | galaxy formation and evolution]] and [[Structure formation | structure formation]]). Many physicists also believe that inflation explains why the universe appears to be the same in all directions ([[Isotropy | isotropic]]), why the [[Cosmic microwave background | cosmic microwave background]] [[Radiation | radiation]] is distributed evenly, why the [[Universe | universe]] is [[Shape of the universe | flat]], and why no [[Magnetic monopole | magnetic monopoles]] have been observed.
- The detailed [[Particle physics | particle physics]] mechanism responsible for inflation is unknown. The basic inflationary paradigm is accepted by most physicists, as a number of inflation model predictions have been confirmed by observation; however, a substantial minority of scientists dissent from this position. The hypothetical [[Field (physics) | field]] thought to be responsible for inflation is called the [[Inflaton | inflaton]].
- In 2002 three of the original architects of the theory were recognized for their major contributions; physicists Alan Guth of M.I.T., Andrei Linde of [[Stanford University | Stanford]], and [[Paul Steinhardt]] of [[Princeton University | Princeton]] shared the prestigious [[Dirac Medal (ICTP) | Dirac Prize]] "for development of the concept of inflation in cosmology". In 2012 Guth and Linde were awarded the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] for their invention and development of inflationary cosmology.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/argumentsforgodsexistence/ontological argument/Ontological argument.md
```markdown
# Ontological argument
- An [[Ontology | ontological]] [[Argument | argument]] is a [[Philosophy | philosophical]] [[Argument | argument]], made from an ontological basis, that is advanced in support of the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. Such arguments tend to refer to the state of [[Existence | being]] or existing. More specifically, ontological arguments are commonly conceived [[A priori and a posteriori | a priori]] in regard to the organization of the universe, whereby, if such organizational structure is true, [[God]] must exist.
- The first [[Ontology | ontological]] argument in [[Western Christianity | Western Christian]] tradition was proposed by [[Anselm of Canterbury | Saint Anselm of Canterbury]] in his 1078 work, [[Proslogion]], in which he defines God as "a [[Existence | being]] than which no greater can be conceived," and argues that such a being must exist in the mind, even in that of the person who denies the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. From this, he suggests that if the greatest possible [[Existence | being]] exists in the mind, it must also exist in reality, because if it existed only in the mind, then an even greater being must be possible—one who exists both in mind and in reality. Therefore, this greatest possible [[Existence | being]] must exist in reality. Similarly, in the East, [[Avicenna | Avicenna's]] [[Proof of the Truthful]] argued, albeit for very different reasons, that there must be a "necessary existent".
- Seventeenth-century French philosopher [[René Descartes]] employed a similar [[Argument | argument]] to Anselm's. Descartes published several variations of his argument, each of which center on the idea that God's [[Existence | existence]] is immediately [[Inference | inferable]] from a "clear and distinct" idea of a supremely perfect [[Existence | being]]. In the early 18th century, [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz | Gottfried Leibniz]] augmented Descartes' ideas in an attempt to prove that a "supremely perfect" being is a coherent concept. A more recent ontological [[Argument | argument]] came from [[Kurt Gödel]], who proposed a formal [[Argument | argument]] for [[God]]'s existence. [[Norman Malcolm]] also revived the ontological argument in 1960 when he located a second, stronger [[Ontology | ontological]] argument in Anselm's work; [[Alvin Plantinga]] challenged this [[Argument | argument]] and proposed an alternative, based on [[Modal logic | modal logic]]. Attempts have also been made to validate Anselm's proof using an [[Automated theorem proving | automated theorem prover]]. Other arguments have been categorised as ontological, including those made by Islamic philosophers [[Mulla Sadra]] and [[Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i | Allama Tabatabai]].
- Just as the ontological [[Argument | argument]] has been popular, a number of criticisms and objections have also been mounted. Its first critic was [[Gaunilo of Marmoutiers]], a contemporary of Anselm's. Gaunilo, suggesting that the [[Ontology | ontological]] argument could be used to prove the existence of anything, uses the analogy of a perfect island. Such would be the first of many parodies, all of which attempted to show the [[Reductio ad absurdum | absurd consequences]] of the ontological [[Argument | argument]]. Later, [[Thomas Aquinas]] rejected the argument on the basis that humans cannot know God's nature. [[David Hume]] also offered an [[Empirical evidence | empirical]] objection, criticising its lack of [[Evidential reasoning approach | evidential reasoning]] and rejecting the idea that anything can exist necessarily. [[Immanuel Kant]]'s critique was based on what he saw as the false premise that [[Existence | existence]] is a predicate, arguing that "existing" adds nothing (including perfection) to the essence of a being. Thus, a "supremely perfect" [[Existence | being]] can be conceived not to exist. Finally, philosophers such as [[C. D. Broad]] dismissed the coherence of a maximally great [[Existence | being]], proposing that some attributes of greatness are incompatible with others, rendering "maximally great being" incoherent.
- Contemporary defenders of the ontological [[Argument | argument]] include Alvin Plantinga, [[Yujin Nagasawa]], and Robert Maydole.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/argumentsforgodsexistence/teleological argument/Teleological argument.md
```markdown
# Teleological argument
- The teleological argument is an argument for the [[Existence of God | existence of God]] or, more generally, that complex functionality in the natural world which looks designed is evidence of an intelligent creator.
- The earliest recorded versions of this argument are associated with [[Socrates]] in [[Ancient Greece | ancient Greece]], although it has been argued that he was taking up an older argument. [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] developed complex approaches to the proposal that the cosmos has an intelligent cause, but it was the [[Stoicism | Stoics]] who, under their influence, "developed the battery of creationist arguments broadly known under the label 'The Argument from Design'".
- [[Abrahamic religions]] have used the teleological argument in many ways, and it has a long association with them. In the [[Middle Ages]], Islamic theologians such as [[Al-Ghazali]] used the argument, although it was rejected as unnecessary by [[Quran | Quranic]] literalists, and as unconvincing by many Islamic philosophers. Later, the teleological argument was accepted by [[Thomas Aquinas | Saint Thomas Aquinas]] and included as the fifth of his "[[Five Ways (Aquinas) | Five Ways]]" of proving the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. In early modern England clergymen such as [[William Turner (naturalist) | William Turner]] and [[John Ray]] were well-known proponents. In the early 18th century, [[William Derham]] published his Physico-Theology, which gave his "demonstration of the being and attributes of God from his works of creation". Later, [[William Paley]], in his 1802 [[Natural Theology or Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity]] published a prominent presentation of the design argument with his version of the [[Watchmaker analogy | watchmaker analogy]] and the first use of the phrase "argument from design".
- From its beginning, there have been numerous criticisms of the different versions of the teleological argument, and responses to its challenge to the claims against non-teleological natural science. Especially important were the general logical arguments made by [[David Hume]] in his [[Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion]], published in 1779, and the explanation of biological complexity given in [[Charles Darwin]]'s [[On the Origin of Species | Origin of Species]], published in 1859. Since the 1960s, Paley's arguments have been influential in the development of a [[Creation science | creation science]] movement which used phrases such as "design by an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]]", and after 1987 this was rebranded as "[[Intelligent design | intelligent design]]", promoted by the [[Intelligent design movement | intelligent design movement]] which refers to an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]]. Both movements have used the teleological argument to argue against the modern scientific understanding of [[Evolution | evolution]], and to claim that supernatural explanations should be given equal validity in the public school science curriculum.
- Also starting already in classical Greece, two approaches to the teleological argument developed, distinguished by their understanding of whether the natural order was literally created or not. The non-creationist approach starts most clearly with Aristotle, although many thinkers, such as the [[Neoplatonism | Neoplatonists]], believed it was already intended by Plato. This approach is not creationist in a simple sense, because while it agrees that a cosmic intelligence is responsible for the natural order, it rejects the proposal that this requires a "creator" to physically make and maintain this order. The Neoplatonists did not find the teleological argument convincing, and in this they were followed by medieval philosophers such as [[Al-Farabi]] and [[Avicenna]]. Later, [[Averroes]] and [[Thomas Aquinas]] considered the argument acceptable, but not necessarily the best argument.
- While the concept of an intelligence behind the natural order is ancient, a rational argument that concludes that we can know that the natural world has a designer, or a creating intelligence which has human-like purposes, appears to have begun with [[Ancient philosophy | classical philosophy]]. Religious thinkers in [[Judaism]], [[Hinduism]], [[Confucianism]], [[Islam]] and [[Christianity]] also developed versions of the teleological argument. Later, variants on the argument from design were produced in [[Western philosophy]] and by [[Christian fundamentalism]].
- Contemporary defenders of the teleological argument are mainly Christians, for example [[Richard Swinburne]] and [[John Lennox]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/argumentsforgodsexistence/teleological argument/Watchmaker analogy.md
```markdown
# Watchmaker analogy
- The [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] [[Analogy | analogy]] or [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] argument is a [[Teleological argument | teleological argument]] used to argue for the pseudoscientific concept of [[Intelligent design | intelligent design]]. The [[Analogy | analogy]] states that a design implies a designer, by an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]], i.e. a [[Creator deity | creator deity]]. The watchmaker analogy was given by [[William Paley]] in his 1802 book [[Natural Theology or Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity]]. The original [[Analogy | analogy]] played a prominent role in [[Natural theology | natural theology]] and the "argument from design," where it was used to support arguments for the existence of [[God]] of the universe, in both [[Christianity]] and [[Deism]]. Prior to Paley, however, [[Isaac Newton | Sir Isaac Newton]], [[René Descartes]], and others from the time of the scientific revolution had each believed "that the physical laws he [each] had uncovered revealed the mechanical perfection of the workings of the universe to be akin to a watch, wherein the [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] is God."
- The 1859 publication of [[Charles Darwin]]'s [[Scientific theory | theory]] of [[Natural selection | natural selection]] put forward an alternative explanation to the watchmaker analogy, for complexity and [[Adaptation | adaptation]]. In the 19th century, deists, who championed the [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] [[Analogy | analogy]], held that Darwin's theory fit with "the principle of [[Uniformitarianism | uniformitarianism]]—the idea that all processes in the world occur now as they have in the past" and that [[Deistic evolution | deistic evolution]] "provided an explanatory framework for understanding species variation in a mechanical universe."
- In the [[United States]], starting in the 1960s, [[Creationism | creationists]] revived versions of the argument to dispute the concepts of [[Evolution | evolution]] and [[Natural selection | natural selection]], and there was renewed interest in the [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] argument. [[Evolutionary biology | Evolutionary biologist]] [[Richard Dawkins]] referred to the [[Analogy | analogy]] in his 1986 book [[The Blind Watchmaker]] giving his explanation of [[Evolution | evolution]]. Others, however, consider the watchmaker analogy to be compatible with [[Evolutionary creation | evolutionary creation]], opining that the two concepts are not mutually exclusive.
```

```markdown
- The earliest recorded versions of this argument are associated with [[Socrates]] in [[Ancient Greece | ancient Greece]], although it has been argued that he was taking up an older argument. - [[Abrahamic religions]] have used the teleological argument in many ways, and it has a long association with them. In the [[Middle Ages]], Islamic theologians such as [[Al-Ghazali]] used the argument, although it was rejected as unnecessary by [[Quran | Quranic]] literalists, and as unconvincing by many Islamic philosophers. Later, the teleological argument was accepted by [[Thomas Aquinas | Saint Thomas Aquinas]] and included as the fifth of his "[[Five Ways (Aquinas) | Five Ways]]" of proving the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. In early modern England clergymen such as [[William Turner (naturalist) | William Turner]] and [[John Ray]] were well-known proponents. In the early 18th century, [[William Derham]] published his Physico-Theology, which gave his "demonstration of the being and attributes of God from his works of creation". Later, [[William Paley]], in his 1802 [[Natural Theology or Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity]] published a prominent presentation of the design argument with his version of the [[Watchmaker analogy | watchmaker analogy]] and the first use of the phrase "argument from design".
- From its beginning, there have been numerous criticisms of the different versions of the teleological argument, and responses to its challenge to the claims against non-teleological natural science. Especially important were the general logical arguments made by [[David Hume]] in his [[Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion]], published in 1779, and the explanation of biological complexity given in [[Charles Darwin]]'s [[On the Origin of Species | Origin of Species]], published in 1859. Since the 1960s, Paley's arguments have been influential in the development of a [[Creation science | creation science]] movement which used phrases such as "design by an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]]", and after 1987 this was rebranded as "[[Intelligent design | intelligent design]]", promoted by the [[Intelligent design movement | intelligent design movement]] which refers to an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]]. Both movements have used the teleological argument to argue against the modern scientific understanding of [[Evolution | evolution]], and to claim that supernatural explanations should be given equal validity in the public school science curriculum.
- Also starting already in classical Greece, two approaches to the teleological argument developed, distinguished by their understanding of whether the natural order was literally created or not. The non-creationist approach starts most clearly with Aristotle, although many thinkers, such as the [[Neoplatonism | Neoplatonists]], believed it was already intended by Plato. This approach is not creationist in a simple sense, because while it agrees that a cosmic intelligence is responsible for the natural order, it rejects the proposal that this requires a "creator" to physically make and maintain this order. The Neoplatonists did not find the teleological argument convincing, and in this they were followed by medieval philosophers such as [[Al-Farabi]] and [[Avicenna]]. Later, [[Averroes]] and [[Thomas Aquinas]] considered the argument acceptable, but not necessarily the best argument.
- While the concept of an intelligence behind the natural order is ancient, a rational argument that concludes that we can know that the natural world has a designer, or a creating intelligence which has human-like purposes, appears to have begun with [[Ancient philosophy | classical philosophy]]. Religious thinkers in [[Judaism]], [[Hinduism]], [[Confucianism]], [[Islam]] and [[Christianity]] also developed versions of the teleological argument. Later, variants on the argument from design were produced in [[Western philosophy]] and by [[Christian fundamentalism]].
- Contemporary defenders of the teleological argument are mainly Christians, for example [[Richard Swinburne]] and [[John Lennox]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/atheism/“You’ve Ruined My Life, Professor Craig!!”  Reasonable Faith.md
```markdown
# “You’ve Ruined My Life, Professor Craig!!” | Reasonable Faith

## Adam's Background and Struggles
- Adam is an atheist who was brought up Catholic but never believed in theism.
- He became interested in philosophy and focused on writing about atheism and God.
- He read Dr. Craig's paper on the absurdity of life without God and wrestled with it.
- He tried to provide answers to Dr. Craig's objections to atheism but now feels he was wrong.

## Adam's Frustration and Desire for Guidance
- Adam finds Dr. Craig's arguments convincing and agrees with him philosophically.
- However, he cannot bring himself to believe in any world religion, including [[Christianity]].
- He feels trapped in a nihilistic-atheistic worldview and has become depressed.
- He is seeking guidance from Dr. Craig, as a philosopher, to help him navigate his beliefs.

## Dr. Craig's Response and Suggestions
- Dr. Craig is encouraged by Adam's letter and compares his journey to C.S. Lewis'.
- He suggests reading Lewis' book "Surprised by Joy" to resonate with the struggle of freeing oneself from atheism.
- Dr. Craig advises seeking experiences that connect with the transcendent and make one open to belief in God, such as beautiful music or nature.
- He recommends reading the Gospels to learn about the life of Jesus and finding them gripping.
- Dr. Craig suggests investigating the historical credibility of Jesus' personal claims and resurrection.
- He proposes beginning to pray daily, attending a [[Christianity | Christian]] church, and getting to know [[Christianity | Christians]].
- Lastly, Dr. Craig recommends reading Francis Thompson's poem "The Hound of Heaven" to recognize God's pursuit and longing.
Overall, Adam is struggling with his atheism and is seeking guidance on how to navigate his beliefs and find meaning. Dr. Craig suggests various steps to help Adam explore his spirituality and consider the rationality of belief in God, particularly through the lens of Christianity.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/atheism/Criticism of religion.md
```markdown
# Criticism of religion
- [[Criticism]] of [[Religion | religion]] involves [[Criticism | criticism]] of the validity, concept, or ideas of [[Religion | religion]].
- Historical records of criticism of religion go back to at least 5th century BCE in [[Ancient Greece | ancient Greece]], in [[Classical Athens | Athens]] specifically, with [[Diagoras of Melos | Diagoras "the Atheist" of Melos]]. In [[Ancient Rome | ancient Rome]], an early known example is [[Lucretius]]' [[De rerum natura]] from the 1st century BCE.
- Every [[Religious exclusivism | exclusive religion]] on Earth (as well as every exclusive world view) that promotes exclusive truth-claims necessarily denigrates the truth-claims of other religions. Thus, some criticisms of [[Religion | religion]] become criticisms of one or more aspects of a specific religious tradition.
- Critics of religion in general may view [[Religion | religion]] as one or more of: outdated, harmful to the [[Individual | individual]], harmful to [[Society | society]], an impediment to the progress of [[Science | science]] or humanity, a source of [[Immorality | immoral]] acts or customs, a political tool for [[Social control | social control]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/atheism/New Atheism.md
```markdown
# New Atheism
- The term New [[Atheism]] was coined by the American journalist [[Gary Wolf (journalist) | Gary Wolf]] in 2006 to describe the positions of some [[Atheism | atheist]] academics, writers, scientists, and philosophers of the 21st century. New Atheism advocates the view that [[Superstition | superstition]], [[Religion | religion]], and [[Irrationalism | irrationalism]] should not simply be tolerated. Instead, they should be [[Criticism of religion | criticised]], [[Antireligion | countered]], examined, and challenged by [[Rationality | rational]] argument, especially when they exert strong influence on the broader society, such as in government, education, and politics. Major figures of New Atheism include [[Richard Dawkins]], [[Sam Harris]], [[Christopher Hitchens]] and [[Daniel Dennett]], collectively referred to as the "[[Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse | four horsemen]]" of the movement, as well as [[Ayaan Hirsi Ali]] until her [[Conversion to Christianity | conversion]] to [[Christianity]] in 2023.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Religious skepticism/J. L. Schellenberg.md
```markdown
# J. L. Schellenberg
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0f/John_Schellenberg_-_Philosophy_at_the_University_of_Edinburgh_%28cropped%29.png)
- John L. Schellenberg (born 1959) is a Canadian philosopher, best known for his work in [[Philosophy of religion | philosophy of religion]]. He has earned a Ph.D. in [[Philosophy]] from the [[University of Oxford]], and is Professor of Philosophy at [[Mount Saint Vincent University]] and Adjunct Professor in the Faculty of Graduate Studies at [[Dalhousie University]], both in [[Halifax, Nova Scotia | Halifax]], [[Nova Scotia]].
- Schellenberg's early development of an [[Argument from nonbelief | argument from divine hiddenness]] for [[Atheism | atheism]] has been influential. In a subsequent series of books he has formulated a hypothetical form of [[Belief | religious belief]] which he has called "[[Religious skepticism | skeptical religion]]", which he regards as being compatible with [[Atheism | atheism]]. In 2013, the [[Cambridge University Press]] journal [[Religious studies | Religious Studies]] published a special issue devoted to critical discussion of Schellenberg's [[Philosophy of religion | philosophy of religion]].
```

```markdown
# Theodore Drange
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ad/Theodore_Drange.jpeg)
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Agnosticism.md
```markdown
# Agnosticism
- Agnosticism is the view or belief that the [[Existence of God | existence of God]], of the [[Divinity | divine]] or the [[Supernatural | supernatural]] is unknown or [[Uncertainty | unknowable]]. Another definition provided is the view that "human reason is incapable of providing sufficient rational grounds to justify either the belief that God exists or the belief that God does not exist."
- The English biologist [[Thomas Henry Huxley]] coined the word agnostic in 1869, and said "It simply means that a man shall not say he knows or believes that which he has no scientific grounds for professing to know or believe." Earlier thinkers, however, had written works that promoted agnostic points of view, such as [[Sanjaya Belatthiputta | Sanjaya Belatthaputta]], a 5th-century BCE [[Ancient philosophy | Indian philosopher]] who expressed agnosticism about any [[Afterlife | afterlife]]; and [[Protagoras]], a 5th-century BCE [[Ancient Greek philosophy | Greek philosopher]] who expressed agnosticism about the existence of "the gods".
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Alvin Plantinga.md
```markdown
# Alvin Plantinga
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9a/Alvin_Plantinga.jpg)
- Alvin Carl Plantinga (born November 15, 1932) is an American [[Analytic philosophy | analytic philosopher]] who works primarily in the fields of [[Philosophy of religion | philosophy of religion]], [[Epistemology | epistemology]] (particularly on issues involving [[Justification (epistemology) | epistemic justification]]), and [[Logic | logic]].
- From 1963 to 1982, Plantinga taught at [[Calvin University]] before accepting an appointment as the John A. O'Brien Professor of Philosophy at the [[University of Notre Dame]]. He later returned to Calvin University to become the inaugural holder of the Jellema Chair in Philosophy.
- A prominent Christian philosopher, Plantinga served as president of the [[Society of Christian Philosophers]] from 1983 to 1986. He has delivered the [[Gifford Lectures]] twice and was described by [[Time (magazine) | Time]] magazine as "America's leading orthodox Protestant philosopher of God". In 2014, Plantinga was the 30th most-cited contemporary author in the [[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]. A fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, he was awarded the [[Templeton Prize]] in 2017.
- Some of Plantinga's most influential works include [[God and Other Minds]] (1967), The Nature of Necessity (1974), and a trilogy of books on [[Epistemology | epistemology]], culminating in [[Warranted Christian Belief]] (2000) that was simplified in Knowledge and Christian Belief (2015).
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Argument from nonbelief.md
```markdown
# Argument from nonbelief
- An [[Argument | argument]] from nonbelief is a [[Argument | philosophical argument]] that asserts an inconsistency between the [[Existence of God | existence of God]] and a world in which people fail to recognize him.  It is similar to the classic [[Problem of evil | argument from evil]] in affirming an inconsistency between the world that exists and the world that would exist if God had certain desires combined with the power to see them through.
- There are two key varieties of the argument.  The argument from reasonable nonbelief (or the [[Argument | argument]] from divine hiddenness) was first elaborated in [[J. L. Schellenberg]]'s 1993 book Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason.  This argument says that if God existed (and was perfectly good and loving) every reasonable person would have been brought to believe in God; however, there are reasonable nonbelievers; therefore, this God does not exist.
- [[Theodore Drange]] subsequently developed the argument from nonbelief, based on the mere existence of nonbelief in God.  Drange considers the distinction between reasonable (by which Schellenberg means inculpable) and unreasonable (culpable) nonbelief to be irrelevant and confusing. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of academic discussion is concerned with Schellenberg's formulation.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Cosmological argument.md
```markdown
# Cosmological argument
- A cosmological argument, in [[Natural theology | natural theology]], is an argument which claims that the existence of [[God]] can be [[Inference | inferred]] from facts concerning [[Causality | causation]], explanation, change, motion, contingency, dependency, or finitude with respect to the [[Universe | universe]] or some totality of objects. A cosmological argument can also sometimes be referred to as an argument from [[Universal causation | universal causation]], an argument from first cause, the causal argument, or [[Unmoved mover | prime mover]] argument. Whichever term is employed, there are two basic variants of the argument, each with subtle yet important distinctions: in esse (essentiality), and in fieri (becoming).
- The basic premises of all of these arguments involve the concept of causation. The conclusion of these arguments is that there exists a first cause, subsequently [[Philosophical analysis | analysed]] to be God. The history of this argument goes back to [[Aristotle]] or earlier, was developed in [[Neoplatonism]] and [[Early Christianity | early Christianity]] and later in medieval [[Schools of Islamic theology | Islamic theology]] during the 9th to 12th centuries, and was re-introduced to medieval Christian theology in the 13th century by [[Thomas Aquinas]]. The cosmological argument is closely related to the [[Principle of sufficient reason | principle of sufficient reason]] as addressed by [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz | Gottfried Leibniz]] and [[Samuel Clarke]], itself a modern exposition of the claim that "[[Nothing comes from nothing | nothing comes from nothing]]" attributed to [[Parmenides]].
- [[Contemporary philosophy | Contemporary]] defenders of cosmological arguments include [[William Lane Craig]], [[Robert C. Koons | Robert Koons]], and [[Alexander Pruss]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Kalam cosmological argument.md
```markdown
# Kalam cosmological argument
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/59/William_Lane_Craig.jpg)
- The [[Kalam]] [[Cosmological argument | cosmological argument]] is a modern formulation of the [[Cosmological argument | cosmological argument]] for the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. It is named after the Kalam (medieval Islamic [[Scholasticism | scholasticism]]), from which its key ideas originated. William Lane Craig was principally responsible for giving new life to the argument in the 20th century, due to his [[The Kalām Cosmological Argument]] (1979), among other writings.
- The argument's key underpinning idea is the [[Metaphysics | metaphysical]] impossibility of [[Actual infinity | actual infinities]] and of a temporally past-infinite universe, traced by Craig to 11th-century Persian Muslim scholastic philosopher [[Al-Ghazali]]. This feature distinguishes it from other cosmological arguments, such as [[Five Ways (Aquinas) | that of Thomas Aquinas]], which rests on the impossibility of a [[Causality | causally]] ordered [[Infinite regress | infinite regress]], and those of [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz | Leibniz]] and [[Samuel Clarke]], which refer to the [[Principle of sufficient reason | principle of sufficient reason]].
- Since Craig's original publication, the Kalam cosmological argument has elicited public debate between Craig and [[Graham Oppy]], [[Adolf Grünbaum]], [[J. L. Mackie]] and [[Quentin Smith]], and has been used in [[Christian apologetics]]. According to [[Michael Lou Martin | Michael Martin]], the cosmological arguments presented by Craig, Bruce Reichenbach, and [[Richard Swinburne]] are "among the most sophisticated and well argued in contemporary [[Theology | theological]] philosophy".
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Natural theology.md
```markdown
# Natural theology
- Natural [[Theology | theology]], once also termed physico-[[Theology | theology]], is a type of theology (similar to [[Deism | deism]], but includes religious ideas besides [[God]]) that seeks to provide arguments for theological topics (such as the [[Existence of God | existence of a deity]]) based on [[Reason | reason]] and the discoveries of [[Science | science]], the project of arguing for the [[Existence of God | existence of God]] on the basis of observed so-called natural facts, and through natural phenomena viewed as divine, or complexities of nature seen as evidence of a divine plan (see [[Predestination | predestination]]) or [[Will of God]],  which includes nature itself.
- This distinguishes it from revealed [[Theology | theology]], which is based on [[Religious text | scripture]] and/or [[Religious experience | religious experiences]], also from [[Transcendental theology | transcendental theology]], which is based on [[A priori and a posteriori | a priori]] reasoning.  It is thus a type of philosophy, with the aim of explaining the nature of the celestial motors, or [[Deity | gods]], or of one supreme god, that are responsible for heavenly motion.  Aristotle's [[Metaphysics (Aristotle) | tractate on metaphysics]] claims to demonstrate the necessary existence of an unmoved [[Unmoved mover | prime mover]].
- For [[Monotheism | monotheistic religions]], this principally involves arguments about the [[Cataphatic theology | attributes]] or [[Apophatic theology | non-attributes]] of a [[Deity | deity]], and especially the deity's existence, using arguments that do not involve recourse to [[Revelation | revelation]].
- The ideals of natural theology can be traced back to the [[Old Testament]] and [[Ancient Greek philosophy | Greek philosophy]]. Early sources evident of these ideals come from [[Jeremiah]] and the [[Book of Wisdom | Wisdom of Solomon]] (c. 50 BC) and [[Plato]]'s dialogue [[Timaeus (dialogue) | Timaeus]] (c. 360 BC).
- [[Marcus Terentius Varro]] (116–27 BCE) established a distinction between [[Political theology | political theology]] (the social functions of religion), natural [[Theology | theology]] and [[Mythical theology | mythical theology]]. His terminology became part of the [[Stoicism | Stoic]] tradition and then [[Christianity]] through [[Augustine of Hippo]] and [[Thomas Aquinas]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Ontological argument.md
```markdown
# Ontological argument
- An [[Ontology | ontological]] [[Argument | argument]] is a [[Philosophy | philosophical]] [[Argument | argument]], made from an ontological basis, that is advanced in support of the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. Such arguments tend to refer to the state of [[Existence | being]] or existing. More specifically, ontological arguments are commonly conceived [[A priori and a posteriori | a priori]] in regard to the organization of the universe, whereby, if such organizational structure is true, [[God]] must exist.
- The first [[Ontology | ontological]] argument in [[Western Christianity | Western Christian]] tradition was proposed by [[Anselm of Canterbury | Saint Anselm of Canterbury]] in his 1078 work, [[Proslogion]], in which he defines God as "a [[Existence | being]] than which no greater can be conceived," and argues that such a being must exist in the mind, even in that of the person who denies the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. From this, he suggests that if the greatest possible [[Existence | being]] exists in the mind, it must also exist in reality, because if it existed only in the mind, then an even greater being must be possible—one who exists both in mind and in reality. Therefore, this greatest possible [[Existence | being]] must exist in reality. Similarly, in the East, [[Avicenna | Avicenna's]] [[Proof of the Truthful]] argued, albeit for very different reasons, that there must be a "necessary existent".
- Seventeenth-century French philosopher [[René Descartes]] employed a similar [[Argument | argument]] to Anselm's. Descartes published several variations of his argument, each of which center on the idea that God's [[Existence | existence]] is immediately [[Inference | inferable]] from a "clear and distinct" idea of a supremely perfect [[Existence | being]]. In the early 18th century, [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz | Gottfried Leibniz]] augmented Descartes' ideas in an attempt to prove that a "supremely perfect" being is a coherent concept. A more recent ontological [[Argument | argument]] came from [[Kurt Gödel]], who proposed a formal [[Argument | argument]] for [[God]]'s existence. [[Norman Malcolm]] also revived the ontological argument in 1960 when he located a second, stronger [[Ontology | ontological]] argument in Anselm's work; [[Alvin Plantinga]] challenged this [[Argument | argument]] and proposed an alternative, based on [[Modal logic | modal logic]]. Attempts have also been made to validate Anselm's proof using an [[Automated theorem proving | automated theorem prover]]. Other arguments have been categorised as ontological, including those made by Islamic philosophers [[Mulla Sadra]] and [[Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i | Allama Tabatabai]].
- Just as the ontological [[Argument | argument]] has been popular, a number of criticisms and objections have also been mounted. Its first critic was [[Gaunilo of Marmoutiers]], a contemporary of Anselm's. Gaunilo, suggesting that the [[Ontology | ontological]] argument could be used to prove the existence of anything, uses the analogy of a perfect island. Such would be the first of many parodies, all of which attempted to show the [[Reductio ad absurdum | absurd consequences]] of the ontological [[Argument | argument]]. Later, [[Thomas Aquinas]] rejected the argument on the basis that humans cannot know God's nature. [[David Hume]] also offered an [[Empirical evidence | empirical]] objection, criticising its lack of [[Evidential reasoning approach | evidential reasoning]] and rejecting the idea that anything can exist necessarily. [[Immanuel Kant]]'s critique was based on what he saw as the false premise that [[Existence | existence]] is a predicate, arguing that "existing" adds nothing (including perfection) to the essence of a being. Thus, a "supremely perfect" [[Existence | being]] can be conceived not to exist. Finally, philosophers such as [[C. D. Broad]] dismissed the coherence of a maximally great [[Existence | being]], proposing that some attributes of greatness are incompatible with others, rendering "maximally great being" incoherent.
- Contemporary defenders of the ontological [[Argument | argument]] include Alvin Plantinga, [[Yujin Nagasawa]], and Robert Maydole.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Problem of evil.md
```markdown
# Problem of evil
- The problem of [[Evil | evil]] is the question of how to reconcile the existence of [[Evil | evil]] and [[Suffering | suffering]] with an [[Omnipotence | omnipotent]], [[Omnibenevolence | omnibenevolent]], and [[Omniscience | omniscient]] [[God]]. There are currently differing definitions of these concepts. The best known presentation of the problem is attributed to the Greek philosopher [[Epicurus]]. It was popularized by [[David Hume]].
- Besides the [[Philosophy of religion | philosophy of religion]], the problem of evil is also important to the fields of [[Theology | theology]] and [[Ethics | ethics]]. There are also many discussions of [[Evil | evil]] and associated problems in other philosophical fields, such as [[Secular ethics | secular ethics]], and [[Evolutionary ethics | evolutionary ethics]]. But as usually understood, the problem of evil is posed in a theological context.
- Responses to the problem of [[Evil | evil]] have traditionally been in three types: refutations, defenses, and [[Theodicy | theodicies]].
- The problem of [[Evil | evil]] is generally formulated in two forms: the logical problem of evil and the evidential problem of evil. The logical form of the argument tries to show a logical impossibility in the coexistence of a god and [[Evil | evil]], while the evidential form tries to show that given the [[Evil | evil]] in the world, it is improbable that there is an omnipotent, omniscient, and a wholly good god. The problem of evil has been extended to non-human life forms, to include [[Suffering | suffering]] of non-human animal species from [[Natural evil | natural evils]] and human [[Cruelty to animals | cruelty]] against them.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Religious epistemology.md
```markdown
# Religious epistemology
- Religious [[Epistemology | epistemology]] broadly covers religious approaches to [[Epistemology | epistemological]] questions, or attempts to understand the epistemological issues that come from religious belief. The questions asked by epistemologists apply to religious beliefs and propositions whether they seem rational, justified, warranted, reasonable, based on evidence and so on. Religious views also influence epistemological theories, such as in the case of [[Reformed epistemology]].
- Reformed epistemology has mainly developed in contemporary Christian religious epistemology, as in the work of [[Alvin Plantinga]] (born 1932), [[William Alston | William P. Alston]] (1921-2009), [[Nicholas Wolterstorff]] (born 1932) and [[Kelly James Clark]], as a critique of and alternative to the idea of "[[Evidentialism | evidentialism]]" of the sort proposed by [[William Kingdon Clifford | W. K. Clifford]] (1845-1879). Alvin Plantinga, for instance, is critical of the evidentialist analysis of knowledge provided by Richard Feldman and by Earl Conee.
- [[Dewi Zephaniah Phillips | D. Z. Phillips]] (1934-2006) states that the argument of the reformed epistemologists furthers and challenges a view he dubs "[[Foundationalism | foundationalism]]":
- The essence of the Reformed challenge is to accuse the foundationalist of claiming to have a criterion of rationality which, in fact, he does not possess. By means of this alleged criterion the foundationalist claims to discern which epistemic practices are rational and which are not. Non-rational practices, he claims, include those of religion.Much work in recent [[Epistemology | epistemology]] of religion goes beyond debates on [[Foundationalism | foundationalism]] and reformed epistemology to consider contemporary issues deriving from social epistemology (especially concerning the [[Epistemology | epistemology]] of testimony, or the epistemology of disagreement), or formal epistemology's use of probability theory. Other notable work draws on the idea that knowing God is akin to knowing a person, which is not reducible to knowing propositions about a person.
- Some work in recent [[Epistemology | epistemology]] of religion discusses various challenges from psychology, cognitive science or evolutionary biology to the rationality or justification of religious beliefs. Some argue that evolutionary explanations of religious belief undermine its rationality. Others respond to these arguments.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Teleological argument.md
```markdown
# Teleological argument
- The teleological argument is an argument for the [[Existence of God | existence of God]] or, more generally, that complex functionality in the natural world which looks designed is evidence of an intelligent creator.
- The earliest recorded versions of this argument are associated with [[Socrates]] in [[Ancient Greece | ancient Greece]], although it has been argued that he was taking up an older argument. [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] developed complex approaches to the proposal that the cosmos has an intelligent cause, but it was the [[Stoicism | Stoics]] who, under their influence, "developed the battery of creationist arguments broadly known under the label 'The Argument from Design'".
- [[Abrahamic religions]] have used the teleological argument in many ways, and it has a long association with them. In the [[Middle Ages]], Islamic theologians such as [[Al-Ghazali]] used the argument, although it was rejected as unnecessary by [[Quran | Quranic]] literalists, and as unconvincing by many Islamic philosophers. Later, the teleological argument was accepted by [[Thomas Aquinas | Saint Thomas Aquinas]] and included as the fifth of his "[[Five Ways (Aquinas) | Five Ways]]" of proving the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. In early modern England clergymen such as [[William Turner (naturalist) | William Turner]] and [[John Ray]] were well-known proponents. In the early 18th century, [[William Derham]] published his Physico-Theology, which gave his "demonstration of the being and attributes of God from his works of creation". Later, [[William Paley]], in his 1802 [[Natural Theology or Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity]] published a prominent presentation of the design argument with his version of the [[Watchmaker analogy | watchmaker analogy]] and the first use of the phrase "argument from design".
- From its beginning, there have been numerous criticisms of the different versions of the teleological argument, and responses to its challenge to the claims against non-teleological natural science. Especially important were the general logical arguments made by [[David Hume]] in his [[Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion]], published in 1779, and the explanation of biological complexity given in [[Charles Darwin]]'s [[On the Origin of Species | Origin of Species]], published in 1859. Since the 1960s, Paley's arguments have been influential in the development of a [[Creation science | creation science]] movement which used phrases such as "design by an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]]", and after 1987 this was rebranded as "[[Intelligent design | intelligent design]]", promoted by the [[Intelligent design movement | intelligent design movement]] which refers to an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]]. Both movements have used the teleological argument to argue against the modern scientific understanding of [[Evolution | evolution]], and to claim that supernatural explanations should be given equal validity in the public school science curriculum.
- Also starting already in classical Greece, two approaches to the teleological argument developed, distinguished by their understanding of whether the natural order was literally created or not. The non-creationist approach starts most clearly with Aristotle, although many thinkers, such as the [[Neoplatonism | Neoplatonists]], believed it was already intended by Plato. This approach is not creationist in a simple sense, because while it agrees that a cosmic intelligence is responsible for the natural order, it rejects the proposal that this requires a "creator" to physically make and maintain this order. The Neoplatonists did not find the teleological argument convincing, and in this they were followed by medieval philosophers such as [[Al-Farabi]] and [[Avicenna]]. Later, [[Averroes]] and [[Thomas Aquinas]] considered the argument acceptable, but not necessarily the best argument.
- While the concept of an intelligence behind the natural order is ancient, a rational argument that concludes that we can know that the natural world has a designer, or a creating intelligence which has human-like purposes, appears to have begun with [[Ancient philosophy | classical philosophy]]. Religious thinkers in [[Judaism]], [[Hinduism]], [[Confucianism]], [[Islam]] and [[Christianity]] also developed versions of the teleological argument. Later, variants on the argument from design were produced in [[Western philosophy]] and by [[Christian fundamentalism]].
- Contemporary defenders of the teleological argument are mainly Christians, for example [[Richard Swinburne]] and [[John Lennox]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/The Religious Experience of Nihilism.md
```markdown
# The Religious Experience of Nihilism

## [[Nihilism]] and the Need for a New Language
- The experience of nihilism is characterized by the belief that all worldly endeavors are futile.
- Discussing nihilism is challenging because there are no words that accurately capture the experience.
- The use of cliches and empty talk hinder a proper understanding of [[Nihilism | nihilism]].
- The experience of nihilism is often described as a dark and unknown tunnel with no clear answers.

## The Silence of the [[Nihilism | Nihilist]]
- Nihilism is an experience that cannot be easily transferred or expressed to others.
- While [[Nihilism | nihilism]] may lead to a Quietist silence, most who experience it do not fully renounce the world.
- The Nihilist focuses on using suicide rather than committing it.
- There is an "affirmative" substance found in nihilism that can be used to develop a language that addresses worldly suffering.
- The concept of God can be seen as a positive expression of [[Nothing | nothingness]].

## The Language of Nihilism
- A new language of [[Nihilism | nihilism]] is needed to confront the Transcendental yearning and avoid falling into naturalistic or religious frameworks.
- The language should not be seen as complete but as a symbolic and self-critical tool.
- Concepts from [[Martin Heidegger | Heidegger]]'s analysis of the human condition can serve as the foundation for a language of nihilism.
- The language should allow for interpretations that vary and leave room for obscurity.

## The Terror of Existence and the Need for Transcendence
- The language of nihilism is not meant to rescue one from nothingness but to confront the nightmare of existence.
- Optimism is seen as a lower form of idolatry that fails to acknowledge the nothingness of the world.
- A language of [[Nihilism | nihilism]] should reconcile the superficial disparities between atheistic and theistic perspectives.
- Naturalistic explanations and traditional conceptions of God are considered inadequate to fully understand the why of existence.

## Criticisms of Unthinking
- Science, when confined to formal descriptions of reality, leads to unthinking and an optimistic scientism.
- Traditional religious interpretations often contain assumptions and answers that shun the mystery of existence.
- Philosophy is needed to open up the mystery of Being instead of closing it off and relying on assumptions.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of religion/Watchmaker analogy.md
```markdown
# Watchmaker analogy
- The [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] [[Analogy | analogy]] or [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] argument is a [[Teleological argument | teleological argument]] used to argue for the pseudoscientific concept of [[Intelligent design | intelligent design]]. The [[Analogy | analogy]] states that a design implies a designer, by an [[Intelligent designer | intelligent designer]], i.e. a [[Creator deity | creator deity]]. The watchmaker analogy was given by [[William Paley]] in his 1802 book [[Natural Theology or Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity]]. The original [[Analogy | analogy]] played a prominent role in [[Natural theology | natural theology]] and the "argument from design," where it was used to support arguments for the existence of [[God]] of the universe, in both [[Christianity]] and [[Deism]]. Prior to Paley, however, [[Isaac Newton | Sir Isaac Newton]], [[René Descartes]], and others from the time of the scientific revolution had each believed "that the physical laws he [each] had uncovered revealed the mechanical perfection of the workings of the universe to be akin to a watch, wherein the [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] is God."
- The 1859 publication of [[Charles Darwin]]'s [[Scientific theory | theory]] of [[Natural selection | natural selection]] put forward an alternative explanation to the watchmaker analogy, for complexity and [[Adaptation | adaptation]]. In the 19th century, deists, who championed the [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] [[Analogy | analogy]], held that Darwin's theory fit with "the principle of [[Uniformitarianism | uniformitarianism]]—the idea that all processes in the world occur now as they have in the past" and that [[Deistic evolution | deistic evolution]] "provided an explanatory framework for understanding species variation in a mechanical universe."
- In the [[United States]], starting in the 1960s, [[Creationism | creationists]] revived versions of the argument to dispute the concepts of [[Evolution | evolution]] and [[Natural selection | natural selection]], and there was renewed interest in the [[Watchmaker | watchmaker]] argument. [[Evolutionary biology | Evolutionary biologist]] [[Richard Dawkins]] referred to the [[Analogy | analogy]] in his 1986 book [[The Blind Watchmaker]] giving his explanation of [[Evolution | evolution]]. Others, however, consider the watchmaker analogy to be compatible with [[Evolutionary creation | evolutionary creation]], opining that the two concepts are not mutually exclusive.
```

```markdown
# William Lane Craig
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/46/Filosof_og_teolog_William_Lane_Craig%2C_2014.jpg)
- William Lane Craig (born August 23, 1949) is an American analytic philosopher, Christian apologist, author, and Wesleyan theologian who upholds the view of [[Molinism]] and [[Apollinarism | neo-Apollinarianism]]. He is currently a Professor of Philosophy at [[Houston Christian University]] and a Research Professor of Philosophy at Biola University's [[Talbot School of Theology]].
- Craig has updated and defended the [[Kalam cosmological argument]] for the [[Existence of God | existence of God]]. He has also published work where he argues in favor of the historical plausibility of the [[Resurrection of Jesus | resurrection of Jesus]]. His study of [[Aseity | divine aseity]] and [[Platonism]] culminated with his book God Over All.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of science/falsifiability/Falsifiability.md
```markdown
# Falsifiability
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/Black_Swans.jpg)
- Falsifiability is a [[Deductive reasoning | deductive]] standard of evaluation of scientific theories and hypotheses, introduced by the [[Philosophy of science | philosopher of science]] [[Karl Popper]] in his book [[The Logic of Scientific Discovery]] (1934). A [[Scientific theory | theory]] or [[Hypothesis | hypothesis]] is falsifiable (or refutable) if it can be logically contradicted by an [[Empirical research | empirical test]].
- Popper proposed falsifiability as the cornerstone solution to both the [[Problem of induction | problem of induction]] and the [[Demarcation problem | problem of demarcation]]. He insisted that, as a logical criterion, falsifiability is distinct from the related concept "capacity to be proven wrong" discussed in Lakatos's falsificationism.  Even being a logical criterion, its purpose is to make the theory [[Predictive power | predictive]] and [[Testability | testable]], and thus useful in practice.
- Popper contrasted falsifiability to the intuitively similar concept of [[Verificationism | verifiability]] that was then current in [[Logical positivism | logical positivism]]. He argues that the only way to verify a claim such as "All swans are white" would be if one could theoretically observe all swans, which is not possible. Instead, falsifiability searches for the anomalous instance, such that observing a single black swan is theoretically reasonable and sufficient to logically falsify the claim. On the other hand, the [[Duhem–Quine thesis]] says that definitive experimental falsifications are impossible and that no scientific [[Hypothesis | hypothesis]] is by itself capable of making predictions, because an [[Empirical research | empirical test]] of the hypothesis requires one or more background assumptions.
- According to Popper there is a clean asymmetry on the logical side and falsifiability does not have the Duhem problem because it is a logical criterion. Experimental research has the Duhem problem and other problems, such as induction, but, according to Popper, statistical tests, which are only possible when a theory is falsifiable, can still be useful within a [[Critical rationalism | critical discussion]].   Philosophers such as [[Deborah Mayo]] consider that Popper "comes up short" in his description of the scientific role of statistical and data models.
- As a key notion in the separation of science from [[Non-science | non-science]] and [[Pseudoscience | pseudoscience]], falsifiability has featured prominently in many scientific controversies and applications, even being used as legal precedent.
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of science/Big Bang.md
```markdown
# Big Bang
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6f/CMB_Timeline300_no_WMAP.jpg)
- The Big Bang event is a [[Theoretical physics | physical theory]] that describes how the [[Expansion of the universe | universe expanded]] from an initial state of high [[Energy density | density]] and [[Temperature | temperature]]. It was first proposed in 1927 by [[Priesthood in the Catholic Church | Roman Catholic priest]] and [[Physicist | physicist]] [[Georges Lemaître]]. Various [[Physical cosmology | cosmological models]] of the Big Bang explain the evolution of the [[Observable universe | observable universe]] from the [[Planck units | earliest known periods]] through its subsequent large-scale form. These models offer a comprehensive explanation for a broad range of observed phenomena, including the abundance of [[Chemical element | light elements]], the [[Cosmic microwave background | cosmic microwave background]] (CMB) [[Electromagnetic radiation | radiation]], and large-scale structure. The overall uniformity of the [[Universe]], known as the [[Flatness problem | flatness problem]], is explained through [[Inflation (cosmology) | cosmic inflation]]: a sudden and very rapid expansion of space during the earliest moments. However, physics currently lacks a widely accepted theory of [[Quantum gravity | quantum gravity]] that can successfully model the earliest conditions of the Big Bang.
- Crucially, these models are compatible with the [[Hubble's law | Hubble–Lemaître law]]—the observation that the farther away a [[Galaxy | galaxy]] is, the faster it is moving away from Earth. Extrapolating this cosmic expansion backwards in time using the known [[Scientific law | laws of physics]], the models describe an increasingly concentrated cosmos preceded by a singularity in which [[Spacetime | space and time]] lose meaning (typically named "the Big Bang singularity"). In 1964 the CMB was discovered, which convinced many cosmologists that the competing [[Steady-state model | steady-state model]] of cosmic evolution was [[Falsifiability | falsified]], since the Big Bang models predict a uniform background radiation caused by high temperatures and densities in the distant past. A wide range of empirical evidence strongly favors the Big Bang event, which is now essentially universally accepted. Detailed measurements of the expansion rate of the [[Universe | universe]] place the Big Bang singularity at an estimated  [[1,000,000,000 | billion]] years ago, which is considered the [[Age of the universe | age of the universe]].
- There remain aspects of the observed universe that are not yet adequately explained by the Big Bang models. After its initial expansion, the [[Universe | universe]] cooled sufficiently to allow the formation of [[Subatomic particle | subatomic particles]], and later [[Atom | atoms]]. The unequal abundances of matter and [[Antimatter | antimatter]] that allowed this to occur is an unexplained effect known as [[Baryon asymmetry | baryon asymmetry]]. These primordial elements—mostly [[Hydrogen | hydrogen]], with some [[Helium | helium]] and [[Lithium | lithium]]—later coalesced through [[Gravity | gravity]], forming early [[Star | stars]] and galaxies. Astronomers observe the gravitational effects of an unknown [[Dark matter | dark matter]] surrounding galaxies. Most of the [[Gravitational potential | gravitational potential]] in the universe seems to be in this form, and the Big Bang models and various observations indicate that this excess [[Gravitational potential | gravitational potential]] is not created by [[Baryon | baryonic matter]], such as normal atoms. Measurements of the redshifts of [[Type Ia supernova | supernovae]] indicate that the **expansion of the universe is accelerating**, an observation attributed to an unexplained phenomenon known as [[Dark energy | dark energy]].
```

##  Philosophy(1)(1)/philosophy of science/Darwinism.md
```markdown
# Darwinism
![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/33/Charles_Darwin_by_Julia_Margaret_Cameron%2C_c._1868.jpg)
- Darwinism is a [[Scientific theory | theory]] of [[Biology | biological]] [[Evolution | evolution]] developed by the English naturalist [[Charles Darwin]] (1809–1882) and others, stating that all [[Species | species]] of organisms arise and develop through the [[Natural selection | natural selection]] of small, inherited variations that increase the individual's ability to compete, survive, and [[Reproduction | reproduce]]. Also called Darwinian theory, it originally included the broad concepts of [[Transmutation of species | transmutation of species]] or of [[Evolution | evolution]] which gained general scientific acceptance after Darwin published [[On the Origin of Species]] in 1859, including concepts which predated Darwin's theories. English biologist [[Thomas Henry Huxley]] coined the term Darwinism in April 1860.
```
